prompt.adult: Hosea says Ephraim has mixed himself among the peoples. What does he then call Ephraim?
prompt.child: The prophet Hosea says Ephraim mixed in with other nations. Then he compares Ephraim to something from the kitchen. What is it?
prompt.teen: In Hosea 7:8, “Ephraim has mixed himself among the peoples; Ephraim is” what?
prompt.older: According to Hosea 7:8, what is Ephraim?

verses.text: “Ephraim has mixed himself among the peoples; Ephraim is a cake unturned.

explanation.adult: Read the end of 7:8, after the second “Ephraim is.”
explanation.child: Look at the last words of verse 8. They come right after “Ephraim is.”
explanation.teen: 7:8 names Ephraim twice. The picture follows the second time, after “is.”
explanation.older: The picture closes 7:8, after the second mention of Ephraim.

teaching.extended_explanation: Hosea 7 describes the northern kingdom, often called Ephraim after its leading tribe, as hot with intrigue and careless of God. 7:8 says Ephraim has mixed himself among the peoples, and then gives a picture of what Ephraim is. 7:9 adds that foreigners have devoured his strength, and he does not know it.
teaching.takeaway: “Ephraim has mixed himself among the peoples; Ephraim is a cake unturned.”

prompt.adult: The LORD asks, “O Ephraim, what shall I do to you? O Judah, what shall I do to you?” What does He say their faithfulness is like?
prompt.child: God asks what He should do with Ephraim and Judah. He says their faithfulness does not last. What does He compare it to?
prompt.teen: In Hosea 6:4, God says, “For your faithfulness is like” what, and like the early dew that goes away?
prompt.older: According to Hosea 6:4, what is the people’s faithfulness like?

verses.text: “O Ephraim, what shall I do to you? O Judah, what shall I do to you? For your faithfulness is like a morning cloud, And like the early dew it goes away.

explanation.adult: Read 6:4 after “For your faithfulness is like.”
explanation.child: In verse 4, find “your faithfulness is like.” The picture comes right after.
explanation.teen: 6:4 gives two pictures of short-lived faithfulness. Read the first, after “is like.”
explanation.older: The first picture in 6:4 follows “For your faithfulness is like,” before the early dew.

teaching.extended_explanation: In 6:1-3 the people speak hopefully of returning to the LORD. In 6:4 God answers with two questions to Ephraim and Judah, then describes their faithfulness with two pictures of things that do not last. The first comes after “is like.”
teaching.takeaway: “Your faithfulness is like a morning cloud, And like the early dew it goes away.”

prompt.adult: Hosea uses a farming picture for Israel’s folly: “They sow the wind.” What does he say they reap (8:7)?
prompt.child: Hosea says the people “sow the wind,” like a farmer planting nothing but air. What does he say they will gather in?
prompt.teen: In Hosea 8:7, “They sow the wind, And reap” what? Compare 10:13, “You have plowed wickedness.”
prompt.older: According to Hosea 8:7, what do those who sow the wind reap?

verses.text: “They sow the wind, And reap the whirlwind. The stalk has no bud; It shall never produce meal. If it should produce, Aliens would swallow it up.
You have plowed wickedness; You have reaped iniquity. You have eaten the fruit of lies, Because you trusted in your own way, In the multitude of your mighty men.

explanation.adult: Read the first sentence of 8:7, right after “And reap.”
explanation.child: Look at the start of verse 8:7. The word comes right after “And reap.”
explanation.teen: 8:7 opens with a sowing and a reaping. Read what follows “reap.”
explanation.older: The first sentence of 8:7 ends with it, after “And reap.”

teaching.extended_explanation: Hosea 8 accuses Israel of making kings without God and idols of silver and gold. 8:7 opens with a farming proverb about sowing and reaping, and adds that the stalk has no bud and produces no meal. 10:13 repeats the farming picture: they plowed wickedness and reaped iniquity.
teaching.takeaway: “They sow the wind, And reap the whirlwind.”

review.notes: Fruitful stage. NKJV excerpt copied from _fruitful_nkjv.json (BibleGateway NKJV). Answer is in the cited verse.

prompt.adult: Israel does not return to the LORD or seek Him (7:10). Instead they call to Egypt and go to Assyria. What does Hosea compare Ephraim to?
prompt.child: Ephraim would not turn back to God. Instead they ran to Egypt and then to Assyria for help. What animal does Hosea compare them to?
prompt.teen: In Hosea 7:11, “Ephraim also is like” what, “without sense”?
prompt.older: According to Hosea 7:11, what is Ephraim like?

verses.text: And the pride of Israel testifies to his face, But they do not return to the LORD their God, Nor seek Him for all this.
“Ephraim also is like a silly dove, without sense— They call to Egypt, They go to Assyria.

explanation.adult: Read 7:11 right after “Ephraim also is like.”
explanation.child: In verse 11, the animal comes right after “Ephraim also is like.”
explanation.teen: 7:11 opens with a comparison. Read what follows “is like,” before “without sense.”
explanation.older: The comparison follows “Ephraim also is like” at the start of 7:11.

teaching.extended_explanation: 7:10 says the pride of Israel testifies against him, yet they do not return to the LORD or seek Him. 7:11 opens with a comparison and then says they call to Egypt and go to Assyria. 7:12 says God will spread His net over them.
teaching.takeaway: “Ephraim also is like a silly dove, without sense.”

prompt.adult: Hosea urges, “Sow for yourselves righteousness; Reap in mercy” (10:12), and later, “Observe mercy and justice” (12:6). What else does 10:12 tell Israel to do, for it is time to seek the LORD?
prompt.child: Hosea tells Israel to plant righteousness and harvest mercy. He gives one more farming command because it is time to seek the LORD. What is it?
prompt.teen: Hosea 10:12 has three farming commands. After “Sow for yourselves righteousness; Reap in mercy,” what is the third?
prompt.older: According to Hosea 10:12, what third command follows “Sow for yourselves righteousness; Reap in mercy”?

choices.text: Gather your stones from the field
Plant your vineyards in the hills
Store your grain in the barns

verses.text: Sow for yourselves righteousness; Reap in mercy; Break up your fallow ground, For it is time to seek the LORD, Till He comes and rains righteousness on you.
So you, by the help of your God, return; Observe mercy and justice, And wait on your God continually.

explanation.adult: Read the third command in 10:12, after “Reap in mercy.”
explanation.child: In verse 10:12, find “Reap in mercy.” The next command comes right after it.
explanation.teen: 10:12 lists three commands. Read the third, before “For it is time.”
explanation.older: The third command follows “Reap in mercy” in 10:12, before “For it is time to seek the LORD.”

teaching.extended_explanation: Hosea often uses farming pictures. 10:12 gives three commands and a reason: it is time to seek the LORD, till He comes and rains righteousness. 10:13 sets the people’s actual sowing against it. In 12:6 the call returns in plain words: return, observe mercy and justice, and wait on God continually.
teaching.takeaway: “Sow for yourselves righteousness; Reap in mercy; Break up your fallow ground.”

prompt.adult: God says He will return to His place till they acknowledge their offense (5:15). Then the people say, “Come, and let us return to the LORD; For He has torn, but He will heal us.” What do they say next (6:1)?
prompt.child: God says He will go away until His people admit their sin. Then they say, “He has torn, but He will heal us.” What do they say right after that?
prompt.teen: Connect Hosea 5:15 and 6:1. In 6:1, “He has stricken, but” what?
prompt.older: According to Hosea 6:1, what will the LORD do, though He has stricken them?

verses.text: I will return again to My place Till they acknowledge their offense. Then they will seek My face; In their affliction they will earnestly seek Me.”
Come, and let us return to the LORD; For He has torn, but He will heal us; He has stricken, but He will bind us up.

explanation.adult: Read the end of 6:1, after “He has stricken, but.”
explanation.child: Look at the last words of verse 6:1. They come right after “He has stricken, but.”
explanation.teen: 6:1 has two contrasts. Read the end of the second one.
explanation.older: The second promise closes 6:1, following “He has stricken, but.”

teaching.extended_explanation: In 5:14-15 God speaks like a lion that tears and goes away, waiting until the people acknowledge their offense and seek His face. 6:1 records their call to return, built on two contrasts: torn but healed, and stricken but restored in a second way at the end of the verse.
teaching.takeaway: “He has stricken, but He will bind us up.”

prompt.adult: In 13:4 the LORD says, “you shall know no God but Me.” In 6:6 He says He desires mercy and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than what?
prompt.child: God told Israel to know no other God but Him. In another place He says He wants mercy more than sacrifice, and knowing God more than something else. What?
prompt.teen: Connect Hosea 13:4 and 6:6. 6:6 says, “For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, And the knowledge of God more than” what?
prompt.older: According to Hosea 6:6, the knowledge of God is desired more than what?

verses.text: For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, And the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
“Yet I am the LORD your God Ever since the land of Egypt, And you shall know no God but Me; For there is no savior besides Me.

explanation.adult: Read the last words of 6:6, right after “the knowledge of God more than.”
explanation.child: Look at the end of verse 6:6. The words come right after “more than.”
explanation.teen: 6:6 has two parallel lines. The second ends after “more than.”
explanation.older: The second line of 6:6 closes with them, after “more than.”

teaching.extended_explanation: 6:6 sums up what God wants, in two parallel lines: mercy rather than sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than what closes the verse. 13:4 reminds Israel that the LORD has been their God since Egypt, and that there is no savior besides Him.
teaching.takeaway: “For I desire mercy and not sacrifice, And the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”

prompt.adult: God says He found Israel like grapes in the wilderness (9:10). In 13:5 He says, “I knew you in the wilderness.” How does He describe that land?
prompt.child: God says finding Israel was like finding grapes in the desert. Later He says He knew them in the wilderness. What kind of land does He say it was?
prompt.teen: Connect Hosea 9:10 and 13:5. In 13:5, “I knew you in the wilderness, In the land of” what?
prompt.older: According to Hosea 13:5, how is the land where God knew Israel described?

verses.text: “I found Israel Like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers As the firstfruits on the fig tree in its first season. But they went to Baal Peor, And separated themselves to that shame; They became an abomination like the thing they loved.
I knew you in the wilderness, In the land of great drought.

explanation.adult: Read the second line of 13:5, after “In the land of.”
explanation.child: Look at the end of verse 13:5. The words come right after “In the land of.”
explanation.teen: 13:5 has two lines. The second ends after “the land of.”
explanation.older: The second line of 13:5 closes with it, after “In the land of.”

teaching.extended_explanation: Twice Hosea looks back to the wilderness years. In 9:10 God remembers finding Israel like grapes in the wilderness and their fathers like the first figs, before they turned to Baal Peor. In 13:5-6 He recalls knowing them in the wilderness, describing the land in the second line, before they were filled and forgot Him.
teaching.takeaway: God says, “I knew you in the wilderness, In the land of great drought.”
